passages.t: Ten brothers go down for grain
passages.happening:
The famine reaches Canaan. Jacob hears that there is grain in Egypt. He says to his sons, “Why are you staring at one another?” (verse 1). “Go down there and buy some for us, so that we may live and not die” (verse 2).

“So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt” (verse 3).

Jacob keeps Benjamin at home, “for he said, ‘I am afraid that harm might befall him’” (verse 4).

The sons of Israel join the crowds of buyers, “since the famine had also spread to the land of Canaan” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
More than twenty years have passed since the brothers sold Joseph. He was seventeen then (37:2). He was thirty when Pharaoh raised him up (41:46). Seven years of plenty have come and gone, and now the famine has begun.

Canaan lived on rain. When the rains failed, the crops failed. Egypt lived on the Nile, which flooded every year from rains far to the south. So in hard years people from Canaan went down to Egypt for food. Abraham did it long before (12:10). ‘Going down’ to Egypt is the usual way the Bible speaks of that road.

Look at the brothers at the start. Their families are hungry, and they stand looking at each other. Their father has to tell them to move.

Notice how the narrator names them. They are ‘Joseph's brothers’, and Benjamin is ‘Joseph's brother’. The missing son is still at the centre of the family, even though no one speaks his name.

And notice Jacob. He sends ten sons into danger, but not Benjamin. Benjamin is Rachel's other son, the only one left. The favoritism that broke this family has not gone away. The ten can see that they are the sons their father is willing to risk.
passages.later:
Stephen tells this part of the story in Acts: “Then famine and great suffering swept across Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food. When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers on their first visit” (Acts 7:11-12).

A psalm sees God's hand in the whole sequence: “He called down famine on the land and cut off all their supplies of food. He sent a man before them” (Psalm 105:16-17).
passages.asks: The brothers stood staring at one another while their families went hungry. Ask whether there is a need in front of you that you have been looking at instead of acting on. Then ask who in your home can see that you love them less than someone else.

passages.happening:
“Now Joseph was the ruler of the land; he was the one who sold grain to all its people. So when his brothers arrived, they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground” (verse 6).

“And when Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but he treated them as strangers and spoke harshly to them” (verse 7). “Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him” (verse 8).

“Joseph remembered his dreams about them and said, ‘You are spies!’” (verse 9). They protest: “Your servants are honest men, not spies” (verse 11). They tell him about their family: twelve brothers, “The youngest is now with our father, and one is no more” (verse 13).

Joseph says they will be tested. They cannot leave unless their youngest brother comes (verses 15-16). “So Joseph imprisoned them for three days” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The dream from chapter 37 comes true in plain sight. The brothers bow with their faces to the ground, just as the sheaves bowed in Joseph's dream (37:7). Only Joseph and the reader know it.

The key word is ‘recognize’. Joseph recognizes them. They do not recognize him. The same Hebrew word was used when the brothers told their father to ‘examine’ the bloody robe (37:32). Now the one they wronged sees them clearly, and they cannot see him at all. He is nearly forty now, shaved like an Egyptian, dressed in linen, speaking Egyptian through an interpreter.

Why would an Egyptian lord suspect spies? Egypt's open side was its north-east corner, the road from Canaan. An Egyptian story from the Middle Kingdom, the Tale of Sinuhe, speaks of the ‘Walls of the Ruler’, border defences built against peoples from that direction. Ten men from Canaan asking about grain could easily look like scouts.

Listen to what the brothers say about the past: ‘one is no more.’ It is a careful way of not saying what happened to him. And Joseph is listening to every word.

Joseph swears ‘as surely as Pharaoh lives’. It is the oath of an Egyptian official, and it helps to hide who he is.
passages.later:
Later Scripture uses the same word for testing that Joseph uses here. A psalm prays, “Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns” (Psalm 139:23).

Jesus, too, was not recognized by his own. John writes, “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him” (John 1:11). After he rose, two of his followers walked with him on the road, “but their eyes were kept from recognizing Him” (Luke 24:16).
passages.hard:
Why is Joseph so harsh? Is he taking revenge?

The text never tells us what is in his heart. It tells us three things: he remembered his dreams (verse 9), he spoke harshly (verse 7), and he wept in private (verse 24). Readers weigh these in different ways.

The most common reading is that Joseph is testing his brothers. He needs to know whether they have changed before he can trust them. His test will set them in the same place they stood twenty years ago: will they leave a brother behind in chains to save themselves, and will they give up Rachel's other son?

Other readers think the story also shows something harsher: a wounded man, with real anger mixed into the testing. That would explain why he first locks all of them up, and then changes his plan. Some add that Joseph wants Benjamin brought so that all eleven brothers will bow, as in his dream.

These readings do not cancel each other out. Genesis shows Joseph as a real man, not a flawless saint. And the tears in verse 24 show that, whatever else he felt, he still loved them.
passages.asks: Joseph knew exactly who his brothers were, and they had no idea who he was. Ask whether there is someone you wronged long ago whom you have stopped thinking about. Then ask whether you would want to be recognized by them today.

passages.happening:
On the third day Joseph changes the plan. “I fear God,” he says (verse 18). One brother will stay in prison. The rest may take grain home, and then bring the youngest brother back (verses 19-20).

The brothers talk among themselves. “Surely we are being punished because of our brother. We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us, but we would not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us” (verse 21).

Reuben says, “Didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy? But you would not listen. Now we must account for his blood!” (verse 22).

“They did not realize that Joseph understood them, since there was an interpreter between them” (verse 23). “And he turned away from them and wept” (verse 24). Then he takes Simeon and has him bound in front of them.
passages.hearers:
‘I fear God.’ To fear God means to take him seriously, to live as someone who will answer to him. An Egyptian lord says it, and the brothers do not guess what it means. It is a hint about who he really is.

Now comes the first honest word the brothers have spoken about Joseph in twenty years. ‘Surely we are being punished because of our brother.’ The Hebrew begins with the word for ‘guilty’: truly we are guilty. No one has accused them of that old crime. A strange lord has accused them of spying. But their own memory goes straight back to the pit.

And we learn something new. Chapter 37 never told us that Joseph cried out. Here we hear it for the first time, through his brothers' guilty memory. ‘We saw his anguish when he pleaded with us.’ They have carried that picture for twenty years.

Reuben answers with ‘I told you so’. He is right that he tried to stop them. But blaming the others is not the same as owning his part. Blood guilt was a heavy idea in their world. Since Abel, shed blood was pictured as crying out to God (4:10).

Joseph hears all of it. They spoke freely, thinking the Egyptian could not understand. He turns away and weeps. Then he turns back and binds Simeon. Simeon was the second son. Perhaps Joseph passes over Reuben because he now knows Reuben had tried to save him.
passages.later:
Scripture often describes buried guilt in this way. Moses warns, “be assured that your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23). A psalm describes the weight of hiding it: “When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). And it describes the release of owning it: “I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity” (Psalm 32:5).

“He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
passages.asks: Twenty years later, the brothers' guilt rose to the surface the moment they were in trouble. Ask whether there is a wrong you have never named aloud. Then ask what it would mean to say it plainly, to God and, if it is safe and right, to the person you wronged.

passages.happening:
Joseph orders his servants to fill the brothers' bags with grain, “to return each man's silver to his sack, and to give them provisions for their journey” (verse 25).

They load their donkeys and leave (verse 26). At the place where they stop for the night, one of them opens his sack to feed his donkey, “and he saw his silver in the mouth of the sack” (verse 27).

“My silver has been returned!” he says. “Their hearts sank, and trembling, they turned to one another and said, ‘What is this that God has done to us?’” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The silver was not coins. Coins came much later. Silver was weighed out in pieces and tied up in a small bundle. Each man finds his own bundle, untouched.

Think about why this frightens them so much. They are already accused of being spies. Now it will look as if they stole from the lord of Egypt too. And there is an older memory. The last time silver changed hands in this story, they took it for their brother (37:28). They went home with silver then too.

For the first time in the Joseph story, the brothers speak of God. ‘What is this that God has done to us?’ They see God's hand, but only as a threat. They do not yet know that the silver is a gift.

The reader knows more than they do. That is what makes these chapters so tense to read.
passages.later: The writer of Hebrews says, “Nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight; everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13). For the guilty brothers, that truth feels like terror. The gospel tells the same truth as the start of mercy: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
passages.asks: The brothers met a gift and felt it as a threat. Ask whether a guilty conscience has ever made you suspicious of kindness. Then ask whether you can believe that God's dealings with you may be mercy, even when they frighten you.

passages.happening:
The brothers come home and tell Jacob what happened (verses 29-34). As they empty their sacks, every man finds his bag of silver, and they are afraid (verse 35).

Jacob says, “You have deprived me of my sons. Joseph is gone and Simeon is no more. Now you want to take Benjamin. Everything is going against me!” (verse 36).

Reuben makes an offer: “You may kill my two sons if I fail to bring him back to you” (verse 37).

Jacob refuses. “My son will not go down there with you, for his brother is dead, and he alone is left” (verse 38). If anything happens to Benjamin, he says, “you will bring my gray hair down to Sheol in sorrow” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
Listen to the brothers' report. It is softer than what happened. They leave out the three days in prison. They do not say that Simeon was tied up in front of them. They are protecting their father, or themselves.

Jacob's words cut. ‘You have deprived me of my sons.’ He blames them for Joseph too. He does not know how right he is.

Then he says ‘his brother is dead, and he alone is left.’ He is speaking of Rachel's sons. He has ten other sons standing in front of him. To him, it is as if Benjamin is the only one.

Reuben's offer is rash. Let his father kill two grandsons? No grandfather would take that. It is a wild promise that solves nothing. Reuben means well again, but once more he cannot lead.

Sheol is the place of the dead. Jacob means that losing Benjamin would kill him.

And notice the irony. ‘Everything is going against me,’ Jacob says. In fact, everything is about to turn for him. Joseph is alive. The food is paid for. God is bringing the family together. But Jacob cannot see it yet.
passages.later:
Paul writes about a God who is at work even when things look the worst: “And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28).

Jesus told of a son who was lost and came home, and a father who ran to him (Luke 15:20). Jacob will have his own day like that, though he cannot believe it yet.
passages.asks: Jacob said ‘Everything is going against me’ at the very moment God was working to save his family. Ask whether you have said the same about your own life. Then ask what it might look like to wait before deciding what God is doing.
